text.p: Britain's National Westminster Bank has yet to explain a 50 million pound ($81.3 million) black hole in its interest rate options book but theories about the loss abound.
Traders were baffled by NatWest's assertion the first half provision revealed on Friday was due to mispricing errors at investment banking arm NatWest Markets, which they said was vague.
The biggest question was how the apparent mispricing went undetected long enough for it to reach such a significant figure.
"If I'd done this the back office would have been on the phone the next day," said a senior derivatives trader at a British bank.

Traders said mispricing could cover a myriad of different circumstances ranging from a simple mis-booking of the trade, where an option was booked as a put when in fact it was a call, to using the wrong pricing model.
This could involve a trader using the right trading tool but consistently getting bad prices, either under- or over-pricing the deals.
Options are contracts which give buyers the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying security at a set price on a set date in the future.
Some reports suggest the derivative at the heart of the affair was a so-called "swaption" which gives, for example, a counterparty the option to swap floating interest rate assets for fixed rates.

Another theory was the trader in question could have either over- or under-estimated the volatility of an option. Traders have discretion over booking what the volatility of a trade was, and this is one of the most common causes of mispricing, traders said.

The loss could simply have been the result of a trader writing the details of the options trade down incorrectly, but this would under normal circumstances be spotted and corrected quickly, either by the trader or a supervisor.

Any of these scenarios could be the result of genuine error, as traders said that any over-the-counter (OTC) option, which would not be traded on an exchange such as LIFFE (London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange), would prove difficult for a back office to price.

The Futures and Options Association (FOA), of which NatWest is a member, advises in its guidelines on derivatives trading that valuations should be carried out independently of those responsible for trade execution.

"If transactions do not have readily available market prices or they are complex, it will be necessary to ensure there that there is a sufficient degree of independent expertise available in the organisation...to value such products" the FOA said.
Otherwise quotations "independent of the product providers" should be available, it added. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
